newsitem.title: NORWAY: FOCUS - Norway's 1997 budget shows huge surplus.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Norway's 1997 budget shows huge surplus.

text.p: Oil-rich Norway unveiled a 1997 draft budget with a 40.9 billion crown ($6.28 billion) surplus on Friday and said its strong economy left it in an enviable situation compared with other European countries.
Despite the huge surplus projected for next year, the government said it would keep a tight grip on the money purse for fear of fuelling inflation.

"The Norwegian economy is in a period of strong growth in terms of employment, production and revenue," Finance Minister Sigbjoern Johnsen said. "If we look at the situation in other European countries, we are in an enviable situation."
The ministry said Norway, which rejected membership of the European Union in 1994, easily fulfilled a key criterion in the EU's Maastricht treaty for monetary union, planned for 1999.

"A general government surplus of 5.1 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is expected in 1997," a statement said. "This figure can be compared with the Maastrict criterion of a deficit ceiling of three percent."
If projected petroleum revenues of 65 billion crowns are excluded, however, next year's budget would have a deficit of 24.2 billion crowns, the ministry said.

Norway, which is the world's largest crude exporter after OPEC giant Saudi Arabia, started running up a budget surplus last year and oil production is expected to remain at more than three million barrels per day for several years to come.
The surplus forecast takes into account an oil price of 125 crowns per barrel this year and 115 crowns per barrel in 1997.
The projected surplus of 40.9 billion crowns will be set aside in the Government Petroleum Fund for investment abroad.
The government has previously emphasised that a substantial share of the projected increase in central government petroleum revenues over the next few years will be ploughed into the fund.
This will reduce Norway's oil dependence and make it easier to meet future welfare obligations for an ageing population.
The ministry said the budget entailed a fiscal tightening equivalent to about one percent of mainland GDP as measured by the non-oil cyclically adjusted budget indicator.
"We got confirmation today that the government is making an effort to contain growth while the economy is at full steam," said Oystein Stephansen, an economist of S-E-Banken, Oslo.

"But with the government going to parliament with such a large surplus it may be difficult for them to get it passed and contain public spending. There is a risk the budget will be watered down," he said.

Central Bank governor Kjell Storvik urged parlament not to dilute the budget and said he shared the government's view that there was a clear risk of further pressure on the economy and higher cost growth next year.
The Labour minority government is under pressure from the opposition right and left of centre to increase expenditure especially in health care before the budget is finally adopted in December.

The government revised upwards 1997 Gross Domestic Product growth at 3.1 percent from 2.3 percent in a previous forecast last May. GDP this year was expected to rise by 5.3 percent compared to the previous forecast of 4.5 percent.
Mainland GDP, which excludes the offshore oil and gas industry, was seen to rise by 3.4 percent this year and 2.5 percent in 1997.
Inflation in 1997 was forecast at 2.5 percent because of higher-than-expected wage agreements this year. The forecast for inflation in 1996 was 1.25 percent.
"Despite strong growth, price inflation has remained subdued, at rates well below that of Norway's main trading partner countries," the ministry said.
Unemployment was seen to fall to 4.0 percent in 1997 from 4.25 percent this year. ($1=6.518 Norwegian Crown)
